speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: asked the Minister for Health what support measures will be granted to persons with disabilities, the young and elderly, who are served with Stay-Home Notice (SHN)/Quarantine Orders (QOs) and are deemed to be unable to do so on their own or in unfamiliar physical settings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Health given how individuals exposed to COVID-19 positive cases serve their SHNs at their place of residence, but those arriving from abroad serve SHN in a dedicated SHN facility, regardless of whether they have access to an isolated place of residence, (a) what are the material differences between these two cases for this differentiated treatment; and (b) whether the Ministry will consider allowing those with isolated residences to serve their SHN at home rather than a dedicated facility, should they opt to do so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the number of confirmed or suspected COVID-19 cases with mild symptoms who sought medical attention at the Emergency Department of a public hospital in the last 28 days; and (b) what are the strategies that the Ministry is considering to direct more of such cases to primary care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Health what are the current procedure and reason for isolating minors issued with a QO, especially with regard to (i) the other members of their household and (ii) their legal guardian.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Health in view of the number of patients hospitalised for COVID-19 (a) what has been the impact on the resources, particularly manpower, allocation within hospitals and the consequent impact on care quality; and (b) how will the Ministry ensure that resources are allocated adequately to those who are ill, including those in critical conditions not related to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health for COVID-19 patients serving their quarantine order at home, whether it is reasonable to expect that, despite their best efforts, they will not spread the virus to members of their household, particularly if they live in smaller flats which lack rooms with attached bathrooms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Those requiring oxygen supplementation or ICU care account for 2% of total cases, most of whom are unvaccinated or the elderly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Occupancy of isolation beds has risen from 58% to 86%, while the occupancy of community care facility (CCF) beds has gone up from 10% to 35%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Public hospital emergency departments have seen up to an eight-fold increase in the number of patients with ART or PCR positive results seeking medical attention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Prior to the last 14 days, we conveyed COVID-19 patients above 70 years old to a hospital within 12 hours from the time they had a PCR positive test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: With the current high caseloads, we are now taking, on average, between 48 and 72 hours to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: SCDF ambulances are reserved for patients with emergency conditions, hence, MOH has set up a dedicated fleet of 95 additional ambulances to convey COVID-19 patients to the different healthcare facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are taking steps to expand our hospital and treatment resources to ensure that everyone who requires medical care, whether for COVID-19 or other conditions, will receive it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have asked hospitals to prioritise resources for COVID-19 patients by reducing non-essential elective appointments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have been shifting asymptomatic and lower-risk COVID-19 patients from hospital to COVID-19 treatment facilities (CTF), as well as the Community Care Facilities (CCFs) and the Home Recovery Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This allows acute hospital resources to be focused on managing patients who need urgent or essential care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: More ICU beds can be opened on short notice, if needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are also closely monitoring the hospital manpower situation, given that close to 400 healthcare workers have tested positive for COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Our hospitals will continue to dynamically cross-deploy their resources to ensure that our manpower needs are met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are also working with private healthcare providers to augment our manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To further preserve our healthcare capacity in the face of future waves of infections, we must also adopt more sustainable healthcare protocols based on the medical care required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Besides focusing our hospital and medical treatment resources on those who need it most, we are also ensuring that our COVID-19 response systems are directed appropriately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to use technology, such as TraceTogether and SafeEntry systems, to automatically and quickly identify the majority of close contacts and to prompt these contacts to self-monitor and take precautions against unknowingly infecting others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This process augments our efforts and allows us to focus the work of the 350 full-time contact tracers that we have today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We must optimise the deployment of these officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As cases have increased multiple fold in the community, it is not always useful to comprehensively contact trace around every case detected by conducting extra interviews and manual case detection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Instead, we are focusing these intensive contact tracing efforts on cases and clusters detected in vulnerable settings like hospitals, nursing homes and schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These are areas where contact mapping and comprehensive identification of close contacts have the greatest public health benefits today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Individuals who are tested positive have also been asked to self-declare their household members so that they can be placed under quarantine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: What we are doing is calling on the self-responsibility of our people to aid our officers and our efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, if I may speak on our quarantine and isolation operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Quarantine Order (QO) and Stay-Home Notice (SHN) processes are administered by around 300 officers from MOH and the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These officers handle around 6,700 daily queries, on average, on issues, such as quarantine status, quarantine conveyance and testing, as well as QO rescindment requests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While such queries should be resolved within three working days, the current surge has resulted in some, especially the complex ones, taking longer to resolve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This also increases the waiting time for others before their calls can be connected, even if their queries are not as complex.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to enhance the resourcing to manage surges and seek the public's understanding of the longer response times during this period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have put out more public communications materials, in print media and on our websites, so that individuals affected by COVID-19 can potentially self-help themselves as well as their families and friends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to scale up the Home Recovery Programme (HRP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This regime places the responsibility on the confirmed COVID-19 cases and their household members, including minors and caregivers to self-register.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Currently, such travellers from Categories II and III countries may already apply to serve their SHN at their place of residence or other suitable accommodation that they have secured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Almost all travellers from Category II countries and around half the travellers from Category III countries fulfill the criteria and have optedout of the dedicated SHN facility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will, progressively, review and adjust our border measures, but, for now, fully vaccinated travellers from Category IV countries must still serve their SHN at the SHN dedicated facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Those serving home quarantine or home SHN are also given information on transmission prevention, including isolation protocols and good personal hygiene practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: ART kits are provided to household members for them to monitor their own health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Those on home isolation requiring dedicated care arrangements may also apply for assistance ahead of, or during the SHN.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Vulnerable persons serving SHN or QO who need support for their activities of daily living, such as minors and the disabled, may also be accompanied by a caregiver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to review our protocols and measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is a financial impact on businesses or individuals whose livelihoods are affected by QOs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: But it remains important that we detect possible COVID-19 infections early, so as to minimise the impact of transmission to their loved ones at home, or to their friends or colleagues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There are some who have a misconception that we are testing widely to attempt to eliminate the virus.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Our widespread testing aims to reduce the overall rate of transmission from each COVID-19 infection, slowing the spread in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: ART testing also enables individuals to perform self-testing and do our own part to slow down transmission of the virus.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These strategies will allow us to ride the wave of infections without overwhelming our healthcare and public health response resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To this end, regular testing in the workplace and at home remains key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have made ART kits widely available, through sale at major retailers, free through nationwide household distributions and supplying kits to companies for mandatory routine testing regimes or voluntary regular testing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Individuals who are exposed to the virus and issued health warnings or alerts may also collect ART kits for regular self-testing from our vending machines island-wide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To make the test kits on sale more competitively priced, we are actively reviewing new brands of equally effective kits to bring into the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will also evaluate if there is a need to conduct another round of nationwide household distribution of kits to support regular self-testing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These fast and easy tests have been effective in augmenting our case identification efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While the Government will continue to make adjustments to augment our healthcare and public health response capacity, all of us need to be socially responsible to take care of ourselves and others around us through regular testing and adherence to isolation protocols if we have been exposed to positive cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Continued adherence to our safe management measures will also help to dampen the rate of transmission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is what it means for us to work together to be a COVID-19 resilient nation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increase in cases and home recovery as the default care management measure for COVID-19 positive cases, there is no discharge memo that will be given after they have recovered, after the 10 days.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What help can individuals get in terms of getting TraceTogether status cleared?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have got quite a few requests for help because many have got their TraceTogether still indicating that they are not cleared and they cannot proceed on to even just do necessary daily activities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The second supplementary question is, for seniors who are sent to the CCF, what is the support given, especially to those who are not so digitally savvy and they need help at the centre?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are alone and are not able to be accompanied and several of them may be over 80.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I also had several requests for help because some of the seniors did not know what to do and even how to ask for help or use some of the simple facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, I have received a lot of feedback, too, where a person, after his discharge, does not have his TraceTogether indication lifted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, once you are infected, the TraceTogether app would know and it will count that 10 days from then, if you are vaccinated, you will be automatically removed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are not vaccinated, it will be, removed after 14 days.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I expect this problem to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for CCF, I thank the Member for raising that issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are nurses and workers available at the CCF.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if we come across such cases where the senior is alone or illiterate, let us know and we will alert the CCFs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are people on hand, medical workers, who can help out and help the senior navigate and understand the messages that we are sending to them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Please limit it to two supplementary questions if possible and keep the questions short.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know it is really a very difficult time for everyone.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We also want to support as much as possible, but I cannot help asking these two supplementary questions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Number one is, thank you for letting us know that Home Recovery now is a default option for COVID-19 positive residents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My questions are specifically for those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What if home recovery is the default option but a resident is just not suitable for recovery at home?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, in the Central district, we have a lot of rental flats where there is a lot of sharing of facilities like toilets and living rooms, with just one door for everybody to get through.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What if the homes are just not suitable for home recovery?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Or what if there are just very large families in some of these homes?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As Members of Parliament, we often get questions that come fast and furious from residents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If the questions come directly to us, we always get responsive replies, especially when we write to MOH officeholders (POHs).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But, in general, how does the public get to know that the caregivers can accompany the more vulnerable, especially if the MOH hotline is very stretched at the moment?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, what if quick responses are required —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the Member could keep her questions short, please.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: — and they just do not know where to get the answers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: HRP is the default, provided you meet certain criteria, such as you are younger, you are vaccinated, some not vaccinated but younger.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But within this default, while it is the default, it is not rigid.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is important that once the person is notified that he is on HRP, he is also given a phone number to call to reach what we call an HRP Buddy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If he is not comfortable because of living conditions or he is living with vulnerable seniors or unvaccinated children, they can then make the request to say, "While I am asked to go on HRP, can I be taken out to a CCF?" And we will try our best to accommodate those requests.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, your residents can certainly, request by calling the HRP Buddy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for how would the public know, mass media is one way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We put out FAQs as simply as we can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But even so, it is hard to understand for many members of the public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Another layer will be our community volunteers, our Community Centres (CCs).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many do call up our CCs to ask questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we also need to arm PA and our CCs with answers for all these questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most, or 80% of the questions, are related to those few things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our volunteers should be also equipped with the information and they can reach out and explain to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has been difficult to call through in the past few days.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we have been beefing up the resources day by day and, with SAF's help, it has really improved a lot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is improving and we continue to improve it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once that happens, as more people can call through, get the answers, they will also tell their friends, and I think the situation will change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Both my supplementary questions have to do with whether we are following a protocol that may look good on the surface but actually seems to make less sense when you dig into the policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first has to do with my question on what are the material differences between importing cases and quarantine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If I may develop this, is the concern the risk of importing new variants?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, does MOH actually have a view on the risks of the new variants' fitness, given that Delta is fairly endemic?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does it make sense to apply such a strict protocol that could discourage business travel with long stay-at-home requirements for imported cases?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question has to do with how the Senior Minister of State indicated that, currently, those issued with a QO should self-isolate, but it actually does not require all family members to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, I wonder what is the Senior Minister of State's view on how this procedure could, potentially, be a loophole, since, surely, there is no appreciable difference between the legal guardian who has to accompany a minor in the case of an SHN versus the other household members, insofar as virus exposure is concerned.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the first question, I think he is, essentially, asking why does it appear as if there are different standards for someone who is travelling, versus someone who is given a Home Quarantine Order or a Health Risk Alert here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if I could go into the specifics of the Member's question or, at least, what I think are the specifics of his question, the risk associated with travellers is partly to do with variants; it is partly to do with the robustness of the information that we are receiving, depending on where they are coming from, what we understand about the situation they have in their home country as well as the particulars of that individual's likely location if they are not in a dedicated facility here, in the stay-at-home facility.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we do take all these factors into account when dealing with the appeals, with respect to travellers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the Member's second question, I did not quite understand what he was asking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, indeed, the risk to the whole household is pretty much the same as a caregiver that accompanies someone who is vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, our request for all of them to register.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, that is why we are requiring the whole household to limit their movement and their exposure to people outside of the household.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And I thank the Minister and the Senior Minister of State for their replies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The COVIDsitrep website is a good initiative in terms of communications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I wish to ask whether the Ministry is prepared to consider a benchmark such as the probability and death rate of getting the seasonal flu and dengue fever versus getting COVID-19, in our public communications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will help allay fears and contextualise the likelihood of getting COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My next supplementary question pertains to Question No 12.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In monitoring the COVID-19 situation in Singapore, I wish to ask the Ministry what the next trigger points that MOH is worried about.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And given the R-naught (R0) indicator, we can roughly predict when they will occur.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, how does MOH intend to communicate both the trigger points as well as the time horizon to the public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will give the public and industries sufficient lead time and early warning to adjust to new measures.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will be putting more information out to the public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But, at the moment, we have not reached that equilibrium yet.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are in the middle of quite a large wave and there are very real anxieties around COVID-19 and, especially for the elderly, the vulnerable, the under-vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I thank the Member for his suggestion that we do need to put some of these numbers in the context of a lot of other diseases that we are used to dealing with.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will do so when we are approaching an equilibrium and we have plans to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But, at the moment, the anxieties are around the large number of cases, the wave that we are experiencing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is very real and we should not underplay it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I understand that Minister Ong Ye Kung will address the second question.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the Member's second question on trigger points before we loosen our safe management measures further, we are aware and we are all well aware that certain countries have declared certain dates or certain vaccination levels, and then, they will open up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because we recognise that in battling COVID-19, this is a live, evolving, fast-changing situation and it is not wise for us to tie our hands and limit our options as we adapt and stay agile in battling the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we will have to take into account of the situation in hospitals, our case numbers, how people are reacting, what is our social preparedness to live with the virus and how businesses are doing, and we adjust our measures from time to time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But our direction is very clear: we have to live with COVID-19, we have to become a COVID-19-resilient nation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The direction is clear, but, from time to time, we may take a longer route, we may take a detour, but we will stay on course.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is far lower than the actual caseload since 19 August.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Delta has been with us for almost six months and there is plenty of data on Delta infections from countries like India and Israel, which were hit by the Delta wave before us.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why was the Government not better prepared for the caseload after reopening?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And for Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, what is the rationale for children under 12 being ineligible for home recovery, given that children, even those unvaccinated, usually have mild or no symptoms when infected?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because allowing them to recover at home, by default, allows their parents to care for them and will also reduce the load on hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not think we characterised our safe management posture as opening and shutting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But depending on the situation, we have to make adjustments and, over time, we have made progress in the sense that I think we have put the circuit breaker behind us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we remember, in April last year, almost all businesses were shut.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, we had Heightened Alert, which is a far more moderate form of slowing transmission, slowing economic activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This time round, we try not to go back to Heightened Alert, but, instead, it is mainly restaurants and F&B that are affected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to keep them open, try not to affect businesses so much.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOF provided financial assistance, but they can operate with table of two.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are making progress and I think we should also feel encouraged that, because of vaccinations, we are able to move forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We were at 100 cases then; if it goes on five times, we would have reached 3,200.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A lot of things were said during the MTF press conferences, but I did refer to it, as, during the preparatory phase, we were hoping to maintain around that number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when the whole thing is over, in the  endemic stage, perhaps, we will see 200 cases, maybe more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I hope we take all these numbers in that spirit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I speak to epidemiologists, doctors all the time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They explain things to me, they cite numbers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I then try to explain things to the public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, some numbers may be picked on, but let us take it in the right spirit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not making any projections or predictions, but these are things that I learn from MOH, and I am trying to explain honestly to the public to the best of my abilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do encourage them to serve home recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And many parents, in fact, like to serve home recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not sure if it is made the default, but, certainly, it has great potential to be made a default.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And a great majority of children can recover very well at home and they are happier that way.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that MOH has tapped on private hospitals to alleviate the load on public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have had residents who have been hospitalised with non-COVID-19 related illnesses and shared that the care was inadequate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I hope the Senior Minister of State can answer that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The whole of our healthcare system has been mobilised for this effort: public and private.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And they are different institutions, but they are working as a team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a bit hard to quantify because the private sector is looking after COVID-19 patients under their roof, but they are also looking after other patients with other conditions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Their doctors and nurses have been deployed elsewhere into other sites.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But to put a specific quantification on it, I do not think I am able to adequately answer the Member's question.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The way I would look at it is this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have a healthcare system here in Singapore that is made up of public and private providers, volunteers as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the healthcare is not just about the bed, doctor or nurse.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is the entire system working together and everyone is mobilised to try to do their best to deal with this crisis in front of us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I suppose the shortest answer to the Member's question is yes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: MOH, currently, publicly, runs regional PCR screening centres.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are not quite located at the convenient locations for those who need to do those tests on a weekly basis or bi-weekly basis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask MOH if there are plans to build more of such centres?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But only the stallholders are allowed to use those testing facilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, in such situations, can MOH allow, support or facilitate these PCR testing facilities to be used by other workers who need to do their regular seven-day, 14-day tests, so that the community resources can be shared and to ensure better convenience for those frontline workers, as well as building that community spirit?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The sector leads among the employers are encouraged to move towards the fast and easy testing RRT, primarily with the employer supervised self-swab model, so that people could self-test at their own location, at their own convenience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some sectors will still keep going with the Quick Test Centres.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is an important part of our strategy going forward for COVID-19 resilience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first is, I take the Minister for Health's earlier explanation about the numbers that were quoted earlier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, my question would be, how many cases were we planning for back then, before this current surge?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And how can we actually put measures in place to make sure that it does not occur, especially when we are planning to loosen the restrictions again in three weeks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I think everybody wants to avoid a situation where we actually end up where, every time we loosen some restrictions, we see a massive surge, and then people cannot actually get any answers, or they cannot get through the hotlines.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second point is whether anything can be done for better communications and messaging for residents and people who are actually affected.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have things like Heightened Alert, Stabilisation, preparatory stages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: People are getting very confused about what each of these actually refer to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Same goes for the acronyms like HRP, QOs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I am sure many Members have actually seen the many, many different flowcharts and spreadsheets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What else can be done to make sure that our communications to a very complicated situation, are communicated to residents so that they do not end up having to jam the hotlines as well?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over 20 months, we have developed many responses, many protocols, in order to handle the situation, which is why there is now a plethora of different protocols.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as I mentioned during our press conference over the weekend, now, we are in a different phase.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many of the protocols were designed at a time when the public wants to see us snuffing out every single cluster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, we have all these tight protocols.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not think we can get away with some abbreviations and some alphabet soup.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is after all, a very complicated situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we will try our best to streamline as much as possible, so that people would understand it, able to do their part to fight against COVID-19 and also, to help others.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Back to the numbers and planning criteria, the Member seems to have a narrative that we totally did not plan for all these.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the contrary, we have always planned for a big surge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You would hear from Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, and these are partners that we work very closely with, they have projected 5,000 and 10,000 cases a day, as high as that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You speak to different epidemiologists, they may have different views, but these are the numbers, if we fully open.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You have seen it in other countries happening that kind of peak.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is why, through our communication with the public, you would hear us – whether myself, Minister Gan Kim Yong or Minister Lawrence Wong – always saying, cases will rise; and when cases rise, the number of people with severe illnesses and deaths will rise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I also mentioned at end August, when we started seeing this wave, we said, that doubling cycle, if it happens five times, we will reach 3,200.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we have always sized ourselves up for that kind of number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We hope that we can do so progressively, and not suddenly, which is why we also announced a four-stage opening process: preparatory stage, where we try out home recovery, build up, our CTFs, CCFs and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then transitions – we call it transition stage one, if people still remember – and stage two, and then, finally, endemicity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We gave no deadline or timeline, for reasons I have explained earlier, that we need to watch the situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we were just in the preparatory stage.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Delta variant came in and then cases started to shoot up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, fortunately, we have always been planning ahead, which is why, at that point in time, we were already ready to handle 1,500 cases a day, in terms of Community Care Facilities (CCFs), hospital beds, ICU beds, and then also thinking already about setting up the Community Treatment Facility (CTF) beds and we are also starting with HRP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, already thinking about the next step on how to handle 10,000 cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in terms of planning capacity, manpower, we are always one, two bounds ahead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And all the complaints about conveyancing, calling, not getting in, people not getting responses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not because the beds were not catered for, but processes with regard to HRP were not totally ready.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are still implementing the pilot programme when all these happened.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the team swung into action, the call of public duty kicked in and everybody was putting in their heart and soul to solve the problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, the hospital capacity that we plan for can focus on the 2% that really need help.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My question pertains to my original Parliamentary Question 18, part (b), which I believe has not been quite answered.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The question really is this: as we learn to live with COVID-19 and settle into a new equilibrium of elevated daily number of cases, in the longer run, what is the capacity of general wards in public hospitals that the Ministry expects to set aside for COVID-19 patients?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The concern is the more beds we set aside for COVID-19 patients,  the less beds we will have for non-COVID-19-related conditions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Are there enough hospital beds to go around in our public healthcare system?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The other side of this question is in terms of wait time to a hospital bed for a COVID-19 patient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the longer run, at steady state, does the Ministry have an expectation and what might that be?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In peacetime, in the endemic situation, we do not have influenza beds, dengue beds or chickenpox beds – and all of these are infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we have are beds on the basis of the patients' needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Increasingly, the COVID-19 patients in hospitals will have other types of diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will have to treat COVID-19 like other infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the most important strategy is to focus the resources that we do have on those who need it the most.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Vaccination is part of reducing the number of people who need those resources.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The well, who are asymptomatic, being able to stay home, or go to CCFs or CTFs, is part of that strategy as well, as are our attempts to then slow down the transmission in the community.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All of these, then, feeds into the issue of wait time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether it is about bed space or having your call answered, making sure that those resources that we have, and those officers, are deployed to deal with the people who need help most, will also help in reducing the wait time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But, ultimately, we do need the manpower and we are working on ramping up that capacity as well.
